An update on regulatory discussions in the U.S. will occur sometime this quarter, according to Chris Boshoff, Pfizer’s chief scientific officer and president of R&D.

By Alison Koo
4 November 2026
Feeder containership charter rates could face downward pressure in 2027 as a wave of newbuild deliveries adds capacity to a market that has enjoyed strong earnings in 2026.
Ship brokerage Intermodal research analyst Vasilis Fousekis noted that the time-charter rate for a 1,700 teu geared feeder had climbed to about $33,750 a day for six to 12 months, up 19% year on year and more than double its 2023 level.
A 1,000 teu vessel now earns approximately $18,750 a day, up 10% annually.
Charterers are fixing sub-3,000 teu tonnage for delivery as far ahead as Q3 27, with average fixture periods extending to around two years.
Linerlytica’s report yesterday disclosed that Namsung Shipping had fixed the newly built 3,318 teu Sheng Shun 62 from Chinese owner Xiamen Hongtai Shipping for $37,000 a day for 23 to 25 months.
Gemini Cooperation partners Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd, in need of tonnage to support their hub-and-spoke model, were also busy. Maersk fixed the 2000-built 2,442 teu Meratus Jayagiri from Indonesian feeder operator Meratus Line for $26,500 a day for two years, while Hapag-Lloyd chartered Germany’s Hanse Bereederung’s 2023-built 1,930 teu Cape Bruno for $21,250 a day for three years.
Market strength has been driven by expanding intra-Asia trade, Middle East disruption, and persistent port congestion.
Mr Fousekis said: “Behind this strength lies a restructuring of Asian trade flows. Product components are now assembled in Vietnam, Malaysia, and Indonesia before onward shipment, adding port calls that favour smaller tonnage.”
However, supply growth presents a more immediate challenge. The feeder orderbook stands at around 1.05m teu, across 635 vessels, equivalent to almost 20% of the existing fleet.
Around 42% of the orderbook capacity is scheduled for delivery in 2027, with another 34% set for 2028, mainly in the 1,000–1,999 teu segment. With demolition remaining negligible, despite 30% of feeder capacity being at least 20 years old, fleet growth could reach around 6% next year.
The outlook is also becoming less favourable with mainline operators set to make a full resumption of Asia-Europe services through the Suez Canal.
Mr Fousekis explained: “The restoration of direct mainline calls at ports such as Jeddah could render some relay services, established during the Cape diversion, redundant as released mid-sized tonnage cascades into regional trades.”

Mercedes-Benz Delays GLC Production in the US From November 2027 to May 2030
33 photos
Photo: Mercedes-AMG
Historically speaking, the GLE midsizer and the more compact GLC are the most popular Mercedes nameplates in the United States of America. The German manufacturer also has an American factory that needs more work, but alas, there is a tariff bill that won't disappear anytime soon.
Mercedes-Benz AG has confirmed that it's delaying GLC production at the Alabama complex from November 2027 to May 2030, leaving the GLC dependent on German production for another two and a half years. This information comes from Automotive News, which underlines that GLC accounts for a quarter of the brand's passenger vehicle sales in the US market.
Almost 54,000 units were sold between January 2026 and September 2026, more than the next three most popular imported Mercs combined. Every one of those German-built models faces a 15% import tariff stateside, eating into their profit margins. Of equal significance, that's a rather expensive way to supply a lucrative market where the GLC already does so well.
Automotive News cites two people familiar with the company's plans, yet a Mercedes spokesperson declined to comment on the revised schedule. What is clear, though, is that Mercedes-Benz AG committed $4 billion to its US manufacturing operations. A key part of that investment is GLC localization, and the delay comes down to costs associated with the generational switchover.
More specifically, the automaker from Stuttgart apparently decided against moving the current GLC to the Vance, Alabama, production facility in favor of waiting for the next generation. Internally referred to as V255, the newcomer should arrive by 2030 because the outgoing 254 series rolled out in 2022.
Photo: Mercedes-AMG Just like the 254, the 255 series is expected with a selection of four- and six-cylinder lumps, along with a choice of plug-in hybrid powertrains. Whether the German automaker will also make a case for V8 muscle, that remains to be seen.
Speaking to the cited publication, Sam Fiorani of AutoForecast Solutions claims that prepping a production complex for a model that is approaching the end of its lifecycle would require another expensive changeover when the next gen drops. Given that every automaker out there is aggressively saving money however possible, Merc's decision makes plenty of sense from a financial standpoint.
Think of it as very sensible planning. As for the import tariff, the situation becomes considerably less attractive for Mercedes-Benz AG. The company will continue importing the GLC from Germany while it waits for the V255. The 15% duty applies to all imported vehicles, giving Mercedes another cost to absorb. And those costs will definitely make a dent in the automaker's financial statements.
Considering that Mercedes hasn't even commented on this purported GLC US production delay, Mercedes has not disclosed how much the delay could add to its tariff bill either. Similarly, we don't know whether Merc intends to offset the expense through higher prices, lower margins, or production efficiencies.
Also known as MBUSI, the Alabama plant currently makes the GLE and GLS lines of sport utility vehicles. The EQE SUV and EQS SUV are made there as well.

7 photos
Photo: KTM
We all knew long before the Esposizione Internazionale Ciclo Motociclo e Accessori (EICMA) kicked off in Milan, Italy, this week, that Austrian bike maker KTM would be there to show off its latest products. We knew about the SX-F Factory Editions and all the other goodies, but what we didn't know was that we'd also be treated to a first look at a brand-new two-wheeler.
Called the 450 RC, the newcomer is aimed straight at the mid-displacement supersport segment, and it throws into the fight all sorts of special equipment, starting with its own chassis setup and ending with its own specifications.
Although it announced the bike in Italy this week, KTM didn't go all in, so we don't have all the specs yet. That's because the model won't enter production before late 2027, making the ride a pure 2028 model year.
The Austrians did reveal a thing or two about the suspension system that will be used on the motorcycle. Truth be told, there are no major surprises there: a WP APEX setup consisting of a 43 mm fork adjustable for compression and rebound at the front, and a shock with the same characteristics at the rear, working in tandem with a single-sided swingarm.
We don't know exactly the specifications of the engine that'll power the KTM 450 RC, but we do know it will be kept in check by a 320 mm front disc with a 4-piston radial WP caliper. The connection to the ground is made through Pirelli Diablo Rosso 4 tires.
KTM also revealed that the motorcycle will be fitted with technologies that are more common on higher-end machines. That includes, among others, cornering ABS, a five-inch TFT screen, and charging ports of both the USB-A and USB-C variety.
We will keep an eye on KTM and report back once we learn more about it – don't expect that to be sooner than the second half of next year, though. Until then, riders on the lookout for new KTM bikes do have something to look forward to, namely the SX-F Factory Editions I mentioned earlier.
Two of them have been shown at the EICMA show in Italy, 450 SX-F Factory Edition and the KTM 250 SX-F Factory Edition. They share a lot of components, including a lighter frame with revised geometry and stiffness, a reworked suspension system, and engine tweaks.
The bike maker promises unprecedented performance from the engines that power these things. The one that gets the 250 SX-F going has been redrawn using lessons learned in MXGP and AMA SMX, while the larger one that powers the 450 SX-F delivers more power than it used to, 64 hp at 10,000 rpm and 52 Nm of torque at 7,000 rpm.
KTM did not reveal when the two new bikes will become available, or how much it will charge for them.

By Charlotte Goldstone
4 November 2026
Carriers are earning up to $1.30 per nautical mile on spot shipments from China to the US west coast, making the transpacific by far the most lucrative major container trade.
Alphaliner’s latest analysis of spot freight revenue per nautical mile highlights the growing gap between the transpacific and other major trades – returns on China-Europe routes are significantly lower, for example.
Spot rates on the Shanghai-USWC route have remained between 3,063 and 3,687 points on the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI) since the beginning of July: at around $7,500 per 40ft, current rates translate into revenue of around $1.30 for each of the 5,775 nautical miles of a voyage to Los Angeles, noted Alphaliner.
Although still below the Covid-era peak of 5,110 SCFI points, recorded in January 2022, rates are at their highest since July 2024, and comparable with those seen during the pandemic boom.
The Shanghai-US East Coast trade is also generating substantial returns, added the analyst, with spot rates remaining above $10,000 per 40ft since late August. This equates to around $0.96 per nautical mile for shipments to New York, via the Panama Canal – comparable with the rates of $10,000-$12,000 recorded between August 2021 and June 2022.
And the carriers have responded to the strength of the Pacific market by increasing capacity, said Alphaliner.
In late August, MSC upgraded its Asia-USWC Sentosa service, replacing 15,000 teu vessels with those of around 23,600 teu. Zim, which already deploys 52% of its capacity on the trade, is preparing to launch another China-California service, the ZX3, next month.
By comparison, Far East-Europe services are generating considerably lower returns. Even using the shorter Suez Canal route, revenue is currently at $0.34 per nautical mile to Rotterdam and $0.50 to Genoa.
For carriers continuing to divert vessels around the Cape of Good Hope to North Europe, revenue per nautical mile falls to $0.26, around 24% less due to the additional 3,309 nautical miles sailed.
Latin American trades offer better returns than Europe, although they remain below the most lucrative North American routes. Shanghai-Santos currently generates $0.42 per nautical mile, while Shanghai-Manzanillo in Mexico yields $0.91.
However, rates on both routes have been volatile over the past six months. Spot rates to Santos have fallen to around half their late-August level, while returns on the Mexico trade have fluctuated between $0.70 and $1.10 per nautical mile.
Alphaliner said strong spot rates reflected the continued absence of spare capacity among the major carriers, with port congestion and schedule disruption preventing fleets from operating efficiently.
Although carriers have begun returning to Suez Canal routings on Asia-Europe services, the consultancy said it saw no immediate signs of overcapacity, and cautioned that revenue per nautical mile did not tell the whole story, as canal charges and insurance premiums also influenced the economics of individual trades.

BMW M 1000 RS Is Not Only a Rennsport Revival, But Also the World’s Most Powerful Hyper Naked
8 photos
Photo: BMW Motorrad
It's a big week for motorcycle lovers all over the world, as everybody who is anybody in this industry has gathered in Milan, Italy, for this year's Esposizione Internazionale Ciclo Motociclo e Accessori (EICMA). The Germans from BMW are there as well, of course, and they've brought along what they themselves describe as the world’s most powerful hyper naked bike.
Starting off from the BMW M 1000 R with the M Competition Package, Motorrad recreated, in some sense, the Rennsport bikes of old, including the RS 255 Kompressor of the 1930s and the BMW RS 54 from later on, but with all the modern twists one would expect from a present-day two-wheeler.
Officially called the M 1000 RS, the bike borrows the water-cooled 999cc four-cylinder in-line engine from the BMW M 1000 RR superbike, which in this application develops 218 hp at 14,500 rpm and 113 Nm of torque at 11,000 rpm. That's plenty of power to make the ride unstoppable, seeing how its empty weight stands at 432 pounds (196 kg) - it reaches 62 mph from a standstill in 3.2 seconds, on to a top speed of 176 mph (283 kph).
Making the RS different from its source bike are a number of dedicated fittings, including an M footrest system and an M seat in Alcantara with RS embroidery that stands 20 mm higher than on the RR, making the bike more front-wheel oriented.
The engine breathes out a special M full titanium exhaust system and spins M carbon wheels that are fitted with M braking components. For aerodynamic purposes, the RS comes with M winglets.
The suspension system is as high-end as you'd expect, with a 45 mm upside-down telescopic fork with dynamic damping control taking care of matters at the front and an aluminum underslung double-sided swingarm doing the same at the back, it too available with dynamic damping control.
As far as the bike's design is concerned, the RS throws into the fight a brushed aluminum fuel tank, matte carbon components, and an aluminum composite bridge frame. Special graphics with RS lettering are also on deck.
BMW said it will only make 1,000 units of the M 1000 RS for global needs, with the first ones expected to hit the market starting March 2027. Over in Germany, Motorrad plans to charge €40,000 for one, VAT included – that would be $45,000 at today’s exchange rates.
Over on the American market, the bike will be offered with slightly different specifications (the hardware setup is, however, the same as on the Old Continent), with the hp levels standing at 205 hp. Over the pond, the ride will arrive in the first quarter of next year, and it will sell significantly cheaper than over in Europe: $38,395.

Plus, the FDA dropped another initiative aimed at accelerating rare disease treatments; HHS greenlights the compounding of six unapproved peptides; and uniQure’s embattled gene therapy for Huntington’s disease has finally been accepted for review.

Big Pharma earnings continued over the past week, with no fewer than a dozen companies reporting third quarter results, including AstraZeneca , Biogen , GSK , Bristol Myers Squibb , Merck , Sanofi , AbbVie and Regeneron .
Pfizer reported flat revenue for the quarter but still beat expectations, pleasing investors. Eli Lilly, meanwhile, made more money with its tirzepatide franchise than Pfizer did across its entire portfolio. Lilly’s sales were so good, in fact, that analysts questioned why the pharma wasn’t better at predicting its own growth.
On the other hand, Alnylam suffered through a tough earnings call , even as the company reported a 59% revenue increase for its transthyretin franchise. CEO Yvonne Greenstreet admitted that the franchise has not been performing as Alnylam had hoped.
On the regulatory front, the FDA issued new draft guidance for the regulation of gene-edited therapies. The “plug and play” strategy would allow one regulatory application to cover gene-editing therapies addressing various disease-causing mutations in a single gene. Analysts flagged Beam Therapeutics and Prime Medicine as two potential beneficiaries of this approach.
Another bit of regulatory news this week was not so well received by industry. A new interim policy from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) essentially allows compounding pharmacies to produce six unapproved peptides . As Robert Popovian, a pharmacist and chief science policy officer at the Global Healthy Living Foundation, wrote in an opinion piece for BioSpace , the policy could not only put Americans in harm’s way but also threaten the overall industry by weakening incentives for rigorous drug development.
And uniQure has finally had an application for its embattled gene therapy for Huntington’s disease accepted for review by the FDA, with an action date of May 1, 2027. May Day is a European festival that marks the beginning of summer. Will it also be the beginning of a disease-modifying treatment for Huntington’s?
